key_insight: Co-designing the attention algorithm with kernel-level pipelining tuned for asymmetric compute/memory characteristics (e.g., Blackwell B200/GB200) recovers lost efficiency from Hopper-optimized implementations, yielding substantially higher throughput and memory efficiency for long‑context attention.
problem_solved: Existing FlashAttention optimizations targeted H100-like (Hopper) hardware and underperform on Blackwell-class GPUs because their compute vs. memory bandwidth tradeoffs are different. This causes suboptimal utilization, higher memory traffic, and worse latency/throughput for large‑context LLM workloads.
method: Algorithm reorganization: tile- and chunk-based attention orderings that reduce memory traffic and enable streaming of Q/K/V blocks rather than full-buffering.
Kernel pipelining: staggered, stage-wise kernels with double-buffering and overlapped compute+DMA to hide memory latency and match the pipeline depth to hardware asymmetry.
Hardware-aware autotuning: select tile sizes, pipeline depth, and precision strategies per device (B200/GB200) to balance compute utilization against memory bandwidth constraints.
impact: Makes attention kernels faster and more memory-efficient on modern Blackwell systems, improving throughput and latency for training and inference of large-context LLMs and lowering operational cost for deployments.
visual_elements: Side-by-side schematic comparing Hopper vs Blackwell hardware asymmetry (compute vs memory bandwidth) and the resulting utilization gap.

paper_title: FlashAttention-4: Algorithm and Kernel Pipelining Co-Design for Asymmetric Hardware Scaling
paper_authors: Ted Zadouri, Markus Hoehnerbach, Jay Shah, Timmy Liu, Vijay Thakkar
